The source initially uses bandwidth/throughput loosely before distinguishing available rate from measured performance. Accept accurate explanations rather than penalizing synonyms alone.
The source uses latency generically. Every assessment specifies one-way latency or RTT explicitly.
The one-bit simplification in P08 is not assessed. Use finite packets and stated assumptions.

P10 contains a dimensional typo in the original displayed calculation: its denominator says 10 x 10^6 Mbps where 10 x 10^6 bits/s is intended. The 20-second result is correct. Preserve the source but use dimensionally correct arithmetic in assessment.
The source uses a simplified three-component delay model. Processing, multi-hop aggregation and advanced queuing models are outside assessment scope.
Queuing is introduced briefly. Questions use given waiting times, basic definition and delay arithmetic; traffic-dependent queue theory is not inferred from this excerpt.

activity.text_alternative: Follow one finite packet in one direction across a single link. Transmission delay is the time needed to put its bits onto the link; propagation delay is the time a signal takes to travel along the cable. The illustrative inputs are a 12000-bit packet, a link rate of 10000000 bits per second, a cable length of 100000 meters, and a propagation speed of 200000000 meters per second. Only cable length is adjustable; all other inputs stay fixed. Compare these two delays separately.
guided_steps: Before changing cable length, predict which delay will change and explain what each delay measures.
Choose another cable length within the range, then compare the displayed transmission and propagation delays with your prediction.
activity.prompt: You connected transmission delay to cable length and propagation delay to packet size. Test that distinction: when only the cable length changes, which delay do you predict will change, and why?
